stops.name: Callao and Lima, the exile received with honors
stops.campa: The Fly raises the island of San Lorenzo and the fortress of the Real Felipe, and O'Higgins lands at Callao: the port of his boyhood voyages, now half-free, half-Spanish, wholly at war. Lima receives the Liberator of Chile with salutes and a house; the government he helped to free by sea votes him honors. He walks streets he walked as the Viceroy's hidden son; the palace his father ruled from stands a musket shot from his lodgings. The canon savors the return of the huacho to the father's city, this time with a liberator's name.

stops.name: Lima, the meeting with Bolívar
stops.campa: Simón Bolívar enters Lima on the first of September 1823 to take up the last campaign of the continental war, and the two liberators meet. At the banquet the Venezuelan raises his glass to the hero of Chacabuco; O'Higgins, who has commanded nations, answers that he comes to serve the freedom of America in whatever rank is given him, as a simple soldier if need be. Miranda's two greatest disciples, the canon observes, close the circle of the Precursor: the one finishing the war the other's fleets made possible.

stops.name: The sierra road, too late for Ayacucho
stops.campa: When Bolívar's army marches into the sierra in 1824, O'Higgins rides after it to serve in the last battle of the American war. He climbs the freezing punas by Jauja toward the theatre of decision, and on the mountain road the couriers meet him with the news: on 9 December, at Ayacucho, Sucre has destroyed the Viceroy's army; the war of three hundred years is over. The canon gives him the exile's peculiar grief: he weeps that America is free and that her last battle was fought without him, turns his horse, and rides back down to the coast a farmer.

stops.name: Hacienda Montalván, Cañete, the planter of the exile
stops.campa: Peru's gratitude gives him the haciendas of Montalván and Cuiba in the warm valley of Cañete, and there the Liberator becomes again what he was on the Laja: a farmer. He plants cane and cotton, doctors his laborers, keeps Chilean wine for Chilean visitors, and writes letter after letter home, to friends, to governments that do not answer, offering his sword in every war Chile fights, urging always one obsession: that Chile must seize and settle the Strait of Magellan before another flag does. Under the fig trees of Montalván, doña Isabel grows old; the canon calls these the years of the long patience.

stops.name: Lima, the death of doña Isabel Riquelme
stops.campa: On 21 April 1839 doña Isabel Riquelme dies in exile, the mother who bore the huacho at eighteen, followed him over the burning cordillera at fifty-six, and kept his house through every banishment. O'Higgins buries her in Lima's earth, far from Chillán, and something of his own root is cut. Rosa remains, the sister-companion of the whole long road. The canon keeps doña Isabel as the silent co-founder of the patria: the woman whose constancy carried the Liberator before the Liberator carried the nation.

stops.name: Montalván and Lima, the restitution and the packed trunks
stops.campa: In 1842 Chile at last turns its face back to him: the government of Bulnes restores the Captain General to the army's rolls with his rank and pay, and letters arrive inviting the Padre de la Patria home. The old man's joy is boyish; he settles his accounts, packs his trunks, and moves down to Lima to take ship for Valparaíso. But his heart, worn out by the long roads, falters as the voyage nears. The doctors forbid the sea. He waits in Lima through the winter, Chile visible, so to speak, from his window, while his strength runs out.

stops.name: Lima, calle Espaderos, 'Magallanes! Magallanes!'
stops.campa: At half past noon on 24 October 1842, in his house on the calle Espaderos, the heart of Bernardo O'Higgins stops. Around the bed stand Rosa, his son Pedro Demetrio, and the Mapuche women who followed him from the Laja twenty years before. In the last labor of his breathing his mind flies not backward to his battles but southward and forward, to the strait at the bottom of the world he has begged Chile to claim, and he cries out the name: Magallanes! Magallanes! Eight months later a Chilean schooner plants the flag on the Strait, obedient to the dying word. The exile's last breath founds a territory.
stops.quote_source: Deathbed tradition, Lima, 24 October 1842, as recorded by those present and preserved by the Chilean Armada and the chroniclers
